source_title: Property Taxation in India: Issues Impacting Revenue Performance and Suggestions for Reform
author_or_org: World Bank (South Asia Urban Unit); cited authors incl. M. Govinda Rao, Simanti Bandyopadhyay
key_finding: India's property tax generates only ~0.2% of GDP versus an OECD average of ~1.1% (one-sixth), and ~3% for Canada/UK/USA where it is the bedrock of local revenue. Actual collection runs just 5-20% of potential (Bengaluru 16%, Jaipur 5%). Property cadasters are 64-81% complete (25-30% of properties unregistered) and collection efficiency is only 30-60% of actual demand. Recommends a state-level Municipal Revenue Board, complete GIS-based property rolls via survey, and reformed valuation.
figure: 0.2% of GDP (India) vs 1.1% OECD avg vs ~3% Canada/UK/USA; collection 5-20% of potential; 25-30% of properties unregistered; collection efficiency 30-60% of demand

key_finding: Property tax revenue formed just ~0.12% of GDP (~0.15% including all municipalities), against ~1.7% for advanced market economies. Property tax is >16% of total revenue and >60% of own tax revenue of Municipal Corporations. About 17% of the 232 Municipal Corporations surveyed reported coverage ratios below 20% (properties paying tax vs estimated properties). MCs' total revenue receipts are only ~0.6% of GDP (2023-24) vs 9.2% (Centre) and 14.6% (States). Diagnoses non-transparent billing and irregular collection.
figure: 0.12-0.15% of GDP vs 1.7% advanced economies; PT = 60%+ of own tax revenue; 17% of 232 MCs have coverage <20%; MC revenue = 0.6% of GDP

key_finding: RBI's first comprehensive municipal-finance report; established that Indian municipal revenues (~1% of GDP) are far below peers (Brazil ~7%, South Africa ~6%), that ULBs depend heavily on devolution/grants rather than own revenue, and flagged property tax under-exploitation as central to municipal fiscal weakness.
figure: Indian municipal revenue ~1% of GDP vs Brazil ~7%, South Africa ~6%

source_title: Property Tax System in India: Problems and Prospects of Reform (NIPFP Working Paper 13-114)
author_or_org: National Institute of Public Finance and Policy (NIPFP)
key_finding: Foundational NIPFP diagnosis. Mathur et al (2009) estimated India's property-tax potential from the 36 million-plus cities at ~0.16-0.24% of GDP, against far lower actual collection. The most important reasons for low collection are poor COVERAGE of the tax base and low COLLECTION EFFICIENCY (Karnataka overall collection efficiency ~62%). Analyses ARV, capital-value and unit-area systems and the manipulation of frozen rental-value rolls.
figure: Estimated potential 0.16-0.24% of GDP; Karnataka collection efficiency ~62%

source_title: Fiscal and distributional implications of property tax reforms in Indian cities (NIPFP WP 06-39)
author_or_org: Simanti Bandyopadhyay & M. Govinda Rao, NIPFP
key_finding: Assessed the fiscal health of major urban agglomerations (Delhi, Hyderabad, Kolkata, Chennai, Pune): most ULBs cannot cover expenditure needs from current revenue; all had unutilised property-tax revenue potential (except Hyderabad); and most would fail to cover expenditure even if full potential were realised. Establishes the structural fiscal gap that under-taxed property entrenches.
figure: All studied UAs (except Hyderabad) had unrealised property-tax potential

source_title: Property Tax Reforms in India: A Comparison of Delhi and Bangalore
author_or_org: Simanti Bandyopadhyay (International Center for Public Policy, Georgia State / NIPFP)
key_finding: Comparative study of the move to Unit Area Value (Delhi) and the self-assessment Unit Area system (Bangalore); finds unit-area methods improved transparency and buoyancy over discretionary ARV but coverage and enforcement gaps persist, and collections remain far below potential in both cities.
figure: Both cities collect well below potential despite unit-area reform

source_title: Report of the High Powered Expert Committee (HPEC) on Investment Estimates in Urban Infrastructure
author_or_org: HPEC, chaired by Isher Judge Ahluwalia (MoUD, Govt of India)
key_finding: Landmark estimate of cumulative urban infrastructure investment need of ~Rs 39.2 lakh crore (~Rs 39,000 billion) at 2009-10 prices for 2012-31. Found Indian urban local governments are 'among the weakest in the world' in capacity to raise resources, with narrow, inflexible tax bases lacking buoyancy. Recommended raising property tax and user charges and strengthening ULB own revenue.
figure: ~Rs 39.2 lakh crore investment need (2012-31); ULBs 'among the weakest in the world' in revenue capacity

author_or_org: Janaagraha Centre for Citizenship and Democracy
key_finding: Diagnostic of the laws/institutions/processes underpinning city governance. ASICS cities generate only ~37% of what they spend (some, e.g. Patna, a fraction); in 11 of 21 cities, salaries rose from 108% to 129% of own revenue (2013-2015). Weak property-tax own-revenue is central to municipal fiscal dependence; ASICS scores cities low on transparency and financial autonomy.
figure: ASICS cities self-generate ~37% of expenditure; salaries up to 129% of own revenue

source_title: Report of the Fifteenth Finance Commission (2021-26)
author_or_org: Fifteenth Finance Commission (N.K. Singh, Chair); summarised by PRS Legislative Research
key_finding: Made property-tax reform a CONDITION of urban grants. Total local-body grants Rs 4,36,361 crore for 2021-26. Entry-level criteria: publish provisional + audited accounts AND states must NOTIFY MINIMUM FLOOR RATES for property tax (operationalised 2021-22; condition for grant eligibility from 2022-23). From 2023-24, growth in property-tax collection must be at least the state's 5-year average GSDP growth. This is the strongest central lever yet tying grants to property-tax effort.
figure: Rs 4,36,361 crore grants conditional on PT floor rates; PT growth must match 5-yr avg GSDP growth from 2023-24

source_title: Bombay HC upholds Capital Value method; strikes down CVS Rules 20, 21, 22 (PIL by Property Owners' Assn etc.)
author_or_org: Bombay High Court (upheld by Supreme Court, 7 Nov 2022); reported LiveLaw / Khaitan & Co
key_finding: On 24 April 2019 the Bombay HC upheld the constitutional validity of Mumbai's shift to the Capital Value System (CVS) but STRUCK DOWN Rules 20, 21, 22 of the 2010/2015 Capital Value Rules as ultra vires the MMC Act for factoring in future development potential / construction possibilities, and barred retrospective application before 20 March 2012. The Supreme Court affirmed on 7 Nov 2022. BMC faced ~Rs 2,300 crore in adjustments. Illustrates how valuation-method reform is fought through litigation by propertied interests.
figure: Rules 20/21/22 struck down; ~Rs 2,300 crore BMC adjustment; SC affirmed 2022

source_title: GIS-Enabled Property Tax Information System (GEPTIS) and GPS property tagging, Bengaluru
author_or_org: BBMP / Greater Bengaluru Authority; reported Citizen Matters, Outlook Money
key_finding: Bengaluru's self-assessment scheme (SAS, since 2008) under unit-area capital value left massive leakage from unauthorised floors/extensions still taxed on original sanctioned plans. GEPTIS GIS mapping served notices to 78,524 undervalued properties for arrears, triggering public backlash and court stay orders. 2024 GPS-tagging campaign aims to digitally map ~25 lakh properties. GBA still faces a ~Rs 3,100 crore revenue shortfall. Shows the promise and political friction of technological property-roll reform.
figure: 78,524 undervalued properties noticed; ~25 lakh to be GPS-tagged; ~Rs 3,100 crore shortfall

source_title: Taxing Immovable Property: Revenue Potential and Implementation Challenges (IMF WP/13/129)
key_finding: Global benchmark study: recurrent property taxes average ~1% of GDP in OECD vs well under 0.5% (often ~0.1-0.2%) in developing economies. Identifies undervaluation, incomplete cadastres and political resistance as universal constraints, and argues property tax is among the most efficient and progressive-capable yet most under-exploited taxes — the analytical underpinning of the India under-collection diagnosis.
figure: OECD recurrent property tax ~1% of GDP vs developing economies often ~0.1-0.2%

source_title: Making the Property Tax Work in Indian Cities
key_finding: Commentary synthesising the RBI 2024 findings: property tax contributes ~0.15% of GDP vs ~1.7% in advanced economies; argues the binding constraints are political-economy (under-assessment protects propertied interests) and administrative (frozen rolls, weak demand-collection), not statutory rates. Advocates GIS rolls, periodic revaluation indexed to market/guidance values, and de-politicised valuation boards.

source_title: What Ails Property Tax in India? Issues and Directions for Reforms
key_finding: Peer-reviewed review attributing chronic under-performance to undervaluation, incomplete coverage, excessive exemptions, weak enforcement and the absence of mandatory periodic revaluation; finds the property tax in India is empirically regressive in incidence and proposes capital-value valuation with GIS-based rolls and a state board.
figure: Property tax incidence found regressive; coverage and revaluation cited as core failures
